title: Notifications docs
intro: Notifications sends WhatsApp, email, SMS, browser push, staff push and webhooks for your website, through your own provider keys. Other products send through it with the Notifications server token pasted into their Connections; your own server sends with the same API. Your website's tokens are in the Portal: open the website, then Install and tokens. The browser token is public and goes into your pages; the server token is secret and stays on your server.
localhost: Testing on your own computer: the browser token also works on pages served from localhost, *.localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1], on any port, over http or https. These pages use your website's real database, keys and providers, so what you send there is sent for real. There is no test mode.
send: Send a message with the server token: POST /v1/messages/<channel> (email, sms, whatsapp, push or staff-push) with the template key, the recipient and the values. The answer (201) is the message as the delivery log keeps it: status sent, queued (waiting for its time), retrying, failed or skipped (unsubscribed, over a send limit, or a product's message you switched off on the channel). Nothing accepted is lost: the message is saved before its first attempt, and an attempt that fails or breaks off (a provider or a database briefly unreachable) answers retrying and is tried again by the retry plan. Send an Idempotency-Key header: the same request again within 24 hours gets the first answer instead of a second message. Send required: true for a message the recipient needs whatever they unsubscribed from (for example an order update from an optional template). Name the values that must never be kept, such as a code or a sign-in link, in secretValues (for example ["code", "link"]): the message is sent with them, and every read of the delivery log (this answer, GET /v1/messages, the delivery-log widget, data-rights exports) shows them hidden (****** or [link hidden]). A send carries up to 50 values of at most 1,000 characters each, 100,000 in all. A product's message may name values that hold long text in longValues (Chat's transcript; the product declares them and adds them to each send): each takes up to 50,000 characters, goes only in the message (never in a subject, title or WhatsApp button), and is sent whole by email; on SMS, WhatsApp and push, and in a subject a template of yours gives it, it is cut to fit the channel at a line or word end, ending with your text message.shortened (Settings → Words and look → Widget texts; "… (shortened)" by default). Your own template keys have no long values.
templates: Templates live in Notifications: one per template key, channel and language, written in the product dashboard (Settings → Templates) or in the template editor widget. Write {name} where a value goes, and {?name}…{/name} around text that shows only when the value name is not empty (for example {?tracking}Track it: {tracking}{/tracking}); sections may hold other sections of other names. A WhatsApp template with a template name at Meta (providerTemplate) may list buttons, [{ index, type, value }]: index is the button's place in the template at Meta (0–9), type is copy_code or url, and value may hold placeholders, for example {code}. A copy-code button copies its value (it is sent as Meta's authentication templates take it, as a url button whose text is the code); a URL button adds its value to the end of its address. Template keys of other products' own messages start with the product id and a dot (for example accounts., chat. or ecommerce.), for every product connected to the Portal, a new one included, and work while the channel is on; every other key is yours (a key with a dot too, when its first part names no product) and needs the Merchant send API feature. Your server reads and changes templates with the server token: GET /v1/templates (the templates of switched-on channels), PUT /v1/templates (one template, with the same checks as the dashboard) and DELETE /v1/templates/<key>/<channel>/<language> (default for the default version); each channel's templates need its feature on, and writes count in the settings API's 60 writes per minute. Each change shows in Recent changes with the signed-in staff member of the call (SS-Sign-In next to the server token). A sensitive template keeps none of its values in the delivery log (they show as ****** or [link hidden]); the templates of Accounts (accounts.…: sign-in codes, magic, reset and setup links) always are, even when saved unchecked. A required message (sign-in codes, order and account updates) is always sent, also to people who unsubscribed by link or keyword (STOP); the templates of Accounts (accounts.…) always are, even when saved unchecked. Any other message is optional and is not sent to people who unsubscribed, unless the send says required: true. Optional templates can use {unsubscribeUrl} (a required template has no unsubscribe link), and only optional emails get one-click unsubscribe headers (an email sent with required: true has none). An urgent message ignores quiet hours; the templates of Accounts (accounts.…) always are, even when saved unchecked.
defaults: Every product ships US-English default templates for the messages it sends (Accounts' sign-in codes, reset, invite and email links; Chat's staff alerts, transcripts and reply alerts; …), so a new website gets them before you write any template. A product's send carries the default words of its message for each channel; Notifications uses them while your website has no template of its own for that key and channel (the recipient's language version, else your default version), and keeps them for the fallback channel. Settings → Templates lists every message your products send, by channel, with its state: Default words, Edited (your version is sent), Switched off, or Not set up. Edit starts from the default words; Reset to default deletes your version, so the default is sent again (versions in other languages stay); Switch off on this channel stops the message there: a send of it is skipped with reason switched_off, shown in the delivery log. Accounts' messages are always sent (switch the sign-in method off in Accounts instead). WhatsApp never has a default: it sends only templates you had approved at Meta. Until you add the WhatsApp template of a product's message with its Meta template name, a send of it on WhatsApp is answered failed with the reason not_set_up (reasonValues names the template key to add), kept in the delivery log, and goes to the fallback channel when you set one (for example WhatsApp, then SMS with its default words). Defaults follow the same rules as your templates: the same {placeholders}, optional sections and limits. The editor names a message's long values (for example Chat's {transcript}, up to 50,000 characters): your template of that message uses them in the message only, never in the subject or a button. Your own server may send defaults with its own keys too (defaults in the send body). A send may also name a fallbackTemplate: while your website has no template of its own for the send's key, your template for the fallback key is used, before the defaults. Ecommerce uses it for its per-status order messages: ecommerce.order_status.<status key> falls back to your general ecommerce.order_status template, then to its default words. Switching either key off on a channel skips the message. A product may also ship its default words in other languages (translations in its messages.json, per channel): a recipient whose language (language, else to.language) has them gets them, the exact language first, then its base language (fr for fr-CA); every other recipient gets the US-English words.
retries: Nothing accepted is lost: a message is saved before its first attempt, and an attempt that fails or breaks off (a provider or a database briefly unreachable) counts as a failed attempt. A message that fails is tried again on the same channel, on the next uses of your website after each wait (there are no background jobs, so on a quiet site it waits for the next request). The Retries setting of each channel picks the waits: short (3 attempts: now, then 1 and 5 minutes later; the default), standard (5 attempts: now, then 1, 5 and 30 minutes and 2 hours later), long (6 attempts: now, then 5 and 15 minutes and 1, 3 and 6 hours later) or custom (your own waits in minutes, up to 10, in Custom waits). A message keeps the waits it was sent with. Then, with the Fallback channel feature, it moves to its fallback channels in order — its template's own list (Settings → Template settings), else the list of its channel (Settings → Fallback channels): email, SMS, WhatsApp or browser push — skipping a channel that is off, where the recipient has no address or unsubscribed, or where no template exists for it. Every attempt is in the delivery log, in your own database.
timing: Quiet hours hold messages that are not urgent until a quiet window ends in the recipient's time zone (to.timeZone, else the time zone in business.json). The windows are the list quiet_hours (Settings → Quiet hours, or GET|PUT /v1/lists/quiet_hours with { value: [{ days: [0-6, 0 = Sunday], from: "21:00", until: "08:00", channels: [] }] }): each holds the channels it names (none: every channel) from a local time until a local time on the weekdays it starts; until at or before from ends the next day. The default is every day from 21:00 until 08:00 on every channel. Send limits skip messages over the hourly or daily cap of messages sent to one recipient; by default they count only optional messages (the setting What the limits count: optional or all), and a template can be always or never counted in its settings. Delayed send takes sendAt (ISO-8601); the message goes out on the first use of your website after that time, so it can be late on a quiet site. Messages of Accounts (accounts.…: sign-in codes, magic, reset and setup links) are always urgent and go at once: neither quiet hours nor sendAt hold them, even when their template is saved unchecked.
languages: With Multi-language templates on, a template can have a version per language. The recipient's language (language, else to.language) picks the version: the exact code, then its base language (pt for pt-BR), else the default version. A WhatsApp template goes to Meta in its version's language as Meta writes it (pt_BR for pt-BR); a default version goes in the WhatsApp setting Language of your Meta templates (en unless you change it).
providers: Connect a provider per channel in the product dashboard (Connections). Email: SMTP, Resend, SendGrid, Mailgun or Amazon SES. SMS: Twilio, or any SMS gateway with an HTTP API. WhatsApp: Meta WhatsApp Cloud API, Twilio, or any WhatsApp gateway with an HTTP API. For a gateway with an HTTP API you build the request: the method (POST, GET, PUT or PATCH), its https address, the body type (json, form, text or none), optional headers as a JSON object and a body template, in the field names your gateway asks for. In the address, the headers and the body, {to} is the number with its country code (+447700900123), {toDigits} the same digits without the + (447700900123), {text} the message, {from} your sender (number or name) and {secret} your key; each is encoded for where it goes. You also say what success is, never guessed from words in the answer: the success statuses (codes, ranges or classes such as 200, 200-204 or 2xx; empty: any 2xx) and, when your gateway answers 200 for a refusal too, the field of its JSON answer that tells (a path such as result.code or data.0.status) and its value on success (for example 0, true or queued). Any other status is a failed attempt (5xx, 408 and 429 are retried); a success status without that value is a failed attempt too (provider_refused). The message id is kept from the path you name (for example data.0.id). Example for an imaginary gateway at gateway.example.com that takes JSON and a bearer key: POST https://gateway.example.com/v1/messages, json, headers {"Authorization": "Bearer {secret}"}, body {"to": "{to}", "text": "{text}"}, success 2xx, id path id. The same gateway with a query string: GET https://gateway.example.com/send?to={toDigits}&msg={text}&key={secret}, body type none, success field ok with value true.
keywords: Unsubscribe keywords: point your provider's incoming-message webhook at the address below. Twilio requests are checked with your auth token; the WhatsApp Cloud API with the app secret (and the verify token for its first check). Any other gateway: give its connection a reply token (at least 16 characters) and say where its incoming request has the sender and the text (a JSON path such as message.from, or a form field), then add ?token=<your reply token> to the address. A reply that is one of the keywords of any language in Settings → Unsubscribe keywords (the list stop_keywords: [{ language, words }]; STOP and UNSUBSCRIBE in English by default) unsubscribes that number from optional messages.
push: Browser push: create a P-256 key pair (VAPID, for example with npx web-push generate-vapid-keys) and enter it in Connections → Push keys. Copy the service worker below to the root of your website as /ss-notifications-sw.js, then place the push-permission widget. When a visitor turns notifications on, the widget fires the ss-notifications:subscribed event on window with { subscriberId } and keeps it in localStorage; send it to your server and link it to your user, then send with to: { subscriberId }. Staff push works the same way in your admin with a ticket (permission push.subscribe); send with to: { staffId } (the user id in the ticket).
webhooks: Outgoing webhooks: add https URLs in Settings → Webhook URLs (5 at most by default; the setting Webhook URLs (at most) takes up to 20), each with the events it takes (none: every event), and a random signing secret (at least 24 characters) in Connections. Your server reads and saves the same list with the server token: GET /v1/lists/webhook_urls and PUT /v1/lists/webhook_urls with { value: [{ url, events }] }, where events lists full types such as message.failed or payments.payment.paid. Each event is a POST of JSON { id, type, createdAt, websiteId, data } with the header SS-Signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "<t>.<body>">. Check it before trusting the body, and refuse times older than 5 minutes. Each delivery is tried again on later uses of your website by the webhooks' Retries setting: standard by default (5 attempts in all: again after 1, 5 and 30 minutes and 2 hours), short, long or custom.
events: Other products' events: with the Notifications server token pasted into their Connections, every product that publishes events (for example payments.payment.paid) forwards each one right after it happens to POST /v1/events with { id, type, at, data } and the event id as its Idempotency-Key. Those events go to the webhook URLs that take their type (or take every event), signed the same way, as Notifications' own events do. The webhook keeps the product's event id as id and its time as createdAt, so your server can match it with that product's GET /v1/events. id (evt_…) and at (ISO-8601) are optional: without them the webhook gets a new id and the time it was received.
log: The delivery log is kept in your own database: forever by default (0), or for the days set in Settings → Delivery log (delivery_log.retentionDays, 1–3650; your database's expiry index removes messages and webhook events that many days after they are sent, failed or skipped, and waiting ones stay). A change applies to messages finished from then on. Why a message was not sent is kept as a code with its values, never as a sentence: reason (with reasonValues) on the message and on each failed attempt, for example provider_status with { status: "503" }, not_set_up with { template } or the skip reasons unsubscribed, limited and switched_off; the delivery-log widget words each code with your widget text reason.<code> (Settings → Words and look → Widget texts), filled with its values. A failed attempt at a provider also keeps the provider's own answer as detail (technical text of at most 200 characters, secrets removed). It never keeps a secret: the values of sensitive templates and those named in secretValues are hidden in its words, values, WhatsApp parameters and buttons, also in data-rights exports. The real words are kept sealed with ENCRYPTION_KEY only while the message still has attempts to make, then cleared; a waiting message whose sealed words no longer open (ENCRYPTION_KEY changed without ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS) fails. Your server reads it with GET /v1/messages?status=&channel=&to=&cursor=&limit= (newest first) and GET /v1/messages/<id>, and counts it with the same filters: GET /v1/messages/count → { count, capped } and GET /v1/messages/counts?by=status|channel|template|source → { total, groups } (a one-off message from your staff counts under template none). The delivery-log widget reads the same with a ticket (log.read) under /v1/admin/messages.
install: Add the script to the pages of your website and place the visitor widget where it should appear. Widgets render nothing while their feature is off or the product is stopped.
admin: Admin widgets run in your own admin with a ticket: the delivery log (log.read), the template editor (templates.edit), send a message (messages.send: a one-off message by email, SMS, WhatsApp or push, transactional or marketing) and staff notifications (push.subscribe). Include the script without data-token, place the widgets and register your ticket function. The widget calls it at start and 1 minute before the ticket expires; your server checks the user's sign-in and role every time.
tickets: Your server asks for a ticket with the server token (never send the server token to a browser). The origin is the address of your admin page: any https origin, or a local one while testing. Tickets last 15 minutes and carry only the permissions of switched-on features.
business: Every product reads your business basics from https://<your domain>/.well-known/business.json. Only name is required; without the file the name is your domain and the time zone is UTC.
api: Routes answer JSON (204 has no body); errors are RFC 9457 problems with a stable code. The reference below says what every call takes and answers. Lists are paged with cursor and limit. Routes of a feature that is off answer 403 feature_off.

build.whatsapp: Nothing on your pages: connect your WhatsApp provider in Connections (Meta WhatsApp Cloud API, Twilio, or any WhatsApp gateway with an HTTP API). WhatsApp has no default words: in Settings → Templates, add the WhatsApp template of each message with its template name approved at Meta; until then a send of it fails (and goes to the fallback channel if you set one). For unsubscribe keywords, point the provider's incoming-message webhook at the WhatsApp address of this guide (Unsubscribe keywords).
build.email: Nothing on your pages: connect your email provider in Connections (SMTP, Resend, SendGrid, Mailgun or Amazon SES) with its sender address. Your products send their emails through it once the Notifications server token is in their Connections; each goes out with its default words until you edit it in Settings → Templates. Optionally set a reply-to address in Settings.
build.sms: Nothing on your pages: connect your SMS provider in Connections (Twilio, or any SMS gateway with an HTTP API). Your products send their messages through it once the Notifications server token is in their Connections; each goes out with its default words until you edit it in Settings → Templates. For unsubscribe keywords (STOP) with Twilio, point its incoming-message webhook at the SMS address of this guide (Unsubscribe keywords).
build.browser_push:
Create a VAPID key pair (for example with npx web-push generate-vapid-keys) and enter it in Connections → Push keys. Copy the service worker of this guide to the root of your website as /ss-notifications-sw.js, then place
with the widget script and your browser token. When a visitor turns notifications on, the ss-notifications:subscribed event on window gives { subscriberId }: send it to your server, keep it with your user, and send with POST /v1/messages/push and to: { subscriberId }.
build.staff_push:
In your admin: copy the service worker of this guide to the root of the site your admin runs on as /ss-notifications-sw.js, and place
with the widget script (without data-token) and your ticket function; your server asks for tickets with POST /v1/tickets and the push.subscribe permission. Staff push uses the same push keys (Connections → Push keys). Send with POST /v1/messages/staff-push and to: { staffId } (the user id in the ticket).
build.webhooks: A receiver on your server for each URL: it takes a POST of JSON { id, type, createdAt, websiteId, data }, checks the SS-Signature header with your signing secret before trusting the body (the check in this guide; refuse times older than 5 minutes) and answers 2xx (anything else is tried again). Add the URLs and the events each takes in Settings → Webhook URLs (or PUT /v1/lists/webhook_urls), and a random signing secret of at least 24 characters in Connections.
build.fallback: Nothing on your pages: in Settings → Fallback channels, list for each channel the channels its failed messages move to, in order (for example WhatsApp, then SMS, then email), and give a template its own list in Template settings when it needs another order (browser push too). Keep those channels on and connected, and send to recipients with several addresses (for example to: { phone, email, subscriberId }); a message moves only to a channel where the recipient has an address and a template exists (yours, or the product's default words).
build.quiet_hours: Nothing on your pages: set the quiet windows in Settings → Quiet hours: the weekdays, from and until (with minutes, in the recipient's time zone) and the channels each one holds. Send each recipient's time zone as to.timeZone (for example America/New_York), else the time zone in your business.json is used. Mark the templates that must never wait as urgent; Accounts' messages always are.
build.send_limits: Nothing on your pages: set how many messages one recipient may get per hour and per day in Settings, and what they count (optional messages only, the default, or all). A send over a cap is answered skipped and shows in the delivery log; a template can be always or never counted in Settings → Template settings.
build.delayed_send: Your server adds sendAt (an ISO 8601 time, for example 2026-12-01T09:00:00Z) to POST /v1/messages/<channel>, at most the days ahead set in Settings (30 by default); a past time sends now. The message waits and goes out on the first use of your website after that time, so it can be late on a quiet site. Accounts' messages always go at once.
build.multi_language: Nothing on your pages: write a version of each template per language in Settings → Templates (or with PUT /v1/templates), and send the recipient's language (language, else to.language, for example fr-FR). The exact code wins, then its base language (fr), else the default version.
build.send_api:
On your server, with the server token: send with POST /v1/messages/ (email, sms, whatsapp, push or staff-push) and an Idempotency-Key header, naming your own template key, the recipient and the values; write those templates in Settings → Templates or with PUT /v1/templates. Read the delivery log with GET /v1/messages. Optionally place the admin widgets in your admin (
, template_editor, send_message) with the widget script and your ticket function (tickets from POST /v1/tickets on your server).

topics: Unsubscribe topics: name the kinds of optional messages your recipients may choose from (Settings → Unsubscribe topics, or GET|PUT /v1/lists/topics with { value: [{ id?, name }] }; a new topic gets its id from its name, and renaming keeps the id), and give each template its topic in Settings → Template settings (the list template_settings: [{ key, topic, fallback, capped }]). An optional message's unsubscribe link ({unsubscribeUrl} and the email List-Unsubscribe header) then names its topic: one click leaves that topic only, and the page lists every topic so the recipient keeps the ones they want or leaves every optional message. Required messages (sign-in codes, order updates) are always sent. Messages carry their topic in the delivery log, and the webhook recipient.unsubscribed names it (topic, null for every optional message).
